sections.heading: C — Focus, vision, night driving, curves, slippery roads, skids and hydroplaning
sections.markdown:
## C — Focus, vision, night driving, curves, slippery roads, skids and hydroplaning

FACT_ID: sec13-F01 | anchor: A163
Turning into a flow of traffic needs a gap long enough to finish the turn and reach the speed of the traffic you are joining without disrupting it. [A163]
Source: [A163 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0163]

FACT_ID: sec13-F02 | anchor: A163
Mindful driving means being mentally present with phone and entertainment off, prepared by scanning ahead, and proactive in adjusting to road, weather and traffic. [A163]
Source: [A163 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0163]

FACT_ID: sec13-F03 | anchor: A163
Your brain can focus on only one thing at a time, so line up your mental attention with where your eyes are looking. [A163]
Source: [A163 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0163]

FACT_ID: sec13-F04 | anchor: A163
Even a distraction lasting a few seconds can have devastating results, so remove distractions from inside and outside the car. [A163]
Source: [A163 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0163]

FACT_ID: sec13-F05 | anchor: A164
Drivers use central, fringe and peripheral vision, and higher speeds lower the quality of all of them. [A164]
Source: [A164 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0164]

FACT_ID: sec13-F06 | anchor: A164
Central vision shows detail straight ahead, fringe vision sees edges without sharp focus, and peripheral vision covers what is off to your side. [A164]
Source: [A164 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0164]

FACT_ID: sec13-F07 | anchor: A165
Your path of travel is the route you drive between places, and you will change it for hazards, weather or a new direction by picturing a new target area. [A165]
Source: [A165 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0165]

FACT_ID: sec13-F08 | anchor: A165
Line of sight is everything between you and the target area you picked, and you switch attention between it and your path of travel quickly and often. [A165]
Source: [A165 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0165]

FACT_ID: sec13-F09 | anchor: A166
Your attention must be shared among your path, line of sight, target area, hazards, your vehicle inside and out, other road users and yourself. [A166]
Source: [A166 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0166]

FACT_ID: sec13-F10 | anchor: A166
Slow down before a sharp curve, on slippery pavement, or when water is on the road so you keep control of the vehicle. [A166]
Source: [A166 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0166]

FACT_ID: sec13-F11 | anchor: A166
At night, drive slowly enough to stop within the reach of your headlights, which is usually 400 feet. [A166]
Source: [A166 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0166]

FACT_ID: sec13-F12 | anchor: A166
Use high beams whenever no vehicles are coming toward you, and switch to regular headlights when traffic approaches. [A166]
Source: [A166 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0166]

FACT_ID: sec13-F13 | anchor: A167
Use regular headlights, not high beams, when you are following another vehicle. [A167]
Why it matters: high beams are dimmed both for oncoming traffic and for the car ahead of you.
Source: [A167 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0167]

FACT_ID: sec13-F14 | anchor: A167
If an oncoming driver keeps high beams on, look toward the right side of the road instead of into the lights. [A167]
Source: [A167 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0167]

FACT_ID: sec13-F15 | anchor: A167
At night, look past your headlight beams for dark shapes and glance to the sides to find the pavement edge and side hazards. [A167]
Source: [A167 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0167]

FACT_ID: sec13-F16 | anchor: A167
Do not wear sunglasses or colored lenses at night or on overcast days, because tinted lenses cut your vision. [A167]
Source: [A167 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0167]

FACT_ID: sec13-F17 | anchor: A167
Lengthen your following distance at night, and especially on unfamiliar roads after dark. [A167]
Source: [A167 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0167]

FACT_ID: sec13-F18 | anchor: A168
Reduce speed before you enter a curve, not in it, to keep traction; uphill curves may need more gas and downhill curves more braking. [A168]
Source: [A168 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0168]

FACT_ID: sec13-F19 | anchor: A168
Approach a curve positioned slightly toward the outside of your lane for more room and a better view around it. [A168]
Source: [A168 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0168]

FACT_ID: sec13-F20 | anchor: A168
Inside a curve, hold a steady speed and steer gently, avoiding sudden braking, sudden acceleration or jerky steering that can upset balance. [A168]
Source: [A168 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0168]

FACT_ID: sec13-F21 | anchor: A168
Leaving a curve, speed up gradually and check your mirrors before merging or changing lanes. [A168]
Source: [A168 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0168]

FACT_ID: sec13-F22 | anchor: A169
Roll is how much the vehicle tilts in a turn and yaw is its side-to-side movement, and adjusting speed and steering balances both in curves. [A169]
Source: [A169 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0169]

FACT_ID: sec13-F23 | anchor: A169
Inertia tries to keep the car going straight, so a sudden turn of the wheel in a curve works against you and steering must be smooth. [A169]
Source: [A169 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0169]

FACT_ID: sec13-F24 | anchor: A169
More speed means more kinetic energy and more time and space needed to stop or turn, so slowing for curves helps you keep traction. [A169]
Source: [A169 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0169]

FACT_ID: sec13-F25 | anchor: A169
Friction between tires and road is what lets you grip, and rain, snow or ice can sharply reduce it in curves, so slow down even more there. [A169]
Source: [A169 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0169]

FACT_ID: sec13-F26 | anchor: A170
On slippery roads you must adjust to conditions, which can mean driving below the posted limit. [A170]
Source: [A170 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0170]

FACT_ID: sec13-F27 | anchor: A170
When rain begins on a hot day, the road is very slippery for the first few minutes because heat brings oil in the asphalt to the surface until it washes off. [A170]
Source: [A170 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0170]

FACT_ID: sec13-F28 | anchor: A170
Snowy roads call for a much larger following distance and a greatly reduced speed. [A170]
Source: [A170 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0170]

FACT_ID: sec13-F29 | anchor: A171
Use snow tires or chains where they are required, and in winter chains or studded tires can improve traction. [A171]
Source: [A171 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0171]

FACT_ID: sec13-F30 | anchor: A171
Shady spots on cold, wet days and bridges or overpasses can be icy even when the rest of the road is not. [A171]
Source: [A171 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0171]

FACT_ID: sec13-F31 | anchor: A171
Ice warming from below freezing to near freezing gets wet on top and becomes even more slippery. [A171]
Source: [A171 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0171]

FACT_ID: sec13-F32 | anchor: A171
Black ice is a thin, hard-to-see coating of ice, so stay alert whenever temperatures are near or below freezing even if you see no ice. [A171]
Source: [A171 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0171]

FACT_ID: sec13-F33 | anchor: A171
A skid happens when tires lose their grip, made more likely by high speed and slick roads when you turn or stop suddenly, and the best defense is avoiding one. [A171]
Source: [A171 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0171]

FACT_ID: sec13-F34 | anchor: A171
In a skid, first lift your foot off the accelerator, then press or pump the brakes; without antilock brakes, stomping the pedal can worsen the skid. [A171]
Source: [A171 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0171]

FACT_ID: sec13-F35 | anchor: A172
During a skid, steer the way the vehicle is moving and keep correcting until the tires regain traction in the direction you steer. [A172]
Source: [A172 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0172]

FACT_ID: sec13-F36 | anchor: A172
Hydroplaning is water building up between tires and road so they lose traction, and slowing down on wet roads is the best prevention. [A172]
Source: [A172 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0172]

FACT_ID: sec13-F37 | anchor: A172
If you hydroplane, lift off the accelerator, brake gently, hold the wheel steady without jerking it, and look where you want to go. [A172]
Why it matters: a skid calls for steering with the slide, but hydroplaning calls for holding the wheel steady.
Source: [A172 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0172]

Glossary: path of travel — the route you drive [A165]. Line of sight — what lies between you and your target area [A165]. Fringe vision — the unfocused edge of what you see [A164]. Black ice — a thin coating of ice that is hard to see [A171]. Hydroplaning — tires riding on a layer of water [A172]. Yaw — side-to-side movement of the vehicle [A169].
Memory aid: for curves remember slow in, steady through, smooth out [A168].
